claim: The study analyzed 100,347 articles from 63 journals between the years 2000-2020.
source: This work characterizes self-citation rates in basic, translational, and clinical Neuroscience literature by collating 100,347 articles from 63 journals between the years 2000–2020.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the dataset size and time period in the abstract.

claim: The study analyzed over five million citations.
source: In analyzing over five million citations, we demonstrate four key findings
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of citations analyzed.

claim: Last Author self-citation rates are increasing relative to First Author self-citation rates.
source: In analyzing over five million citations, we demonstrate four key findings: (1) increasing self-citation rates of Last Authors relative to First Authors
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Low- and middle-income countries have lower self-citation rates.
source: In analyzing over five million citations, we demonstrate four key findings: (1) increasing self-citation rates of Last Authors relative to First Authors, (2) lower self-citation rates in low- and middle-income countries
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract and supported by data analysis in the manuscript.

claim: Gender differences in self-citation stem from differences in the number of previously published papers.
source: In analyzing over five million citations, we demonstrate four key findings: (1) increasing self-citation rates of Last Authors relative to First Authors, (2) lower self-citation rates in low- and middle-income countries, (3) gender differences in self-citation stemming from differences in the number of previously published papers
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract and supported by statistical modeling in the manuscript.

claim: Self-citation rates vary by field.
source: In analyzing over five million citations, we demonstrate four key findings: (1) increasing self-citation rates of Last Authors relative to First Authors, (2) lower self-citation rates in low- and middle-income countries, (3) gender differences in self-citation stemming from differences in the number of previously published papers, and (4) variations in self-citation rates by field.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract and supported by field-specific analysis in the manuscript.

claim: Citation counts and metrics like the h-index are critical for hiring and promotion in academia.
source: Furthermore, citation counts and other metrics like the h-index are critical for hiring and promotion in an increasingly tenuous academic job market (Abbott, 2010; Else, 2021; Holden et al., 2005), necessitating a thorough examination of citation practices across research fields.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The decrease in First Author relative to Last Author self-citations since 2000 could make it harder for early-career scientists to advance in their academic careers.
source: A more concerning trend is the decrease in First Author relative to Last Author self-citations since 2000. In the Neurosciences, First Authors are typically early-career researchers (e.g. graduate students, postdoctoral fellows) who perform the majority of the experiments and analysis, whereas Last Authors are typically professors who oversee the project and secure funding. As a result, these changes in citation practices could make it harder for early-career scientists to advance in their academic careers, warranting further investigation and monitoring.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation and potential implication of the observed trend.
